pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Drawing Ray Diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics, 'Light waves' + Working Scientifically):** "use of ray model to explain imaging in mirrors, the pinhole camera, the refraction of light and action of convex lens in focusing (qualitative)." Because this topic is the DRAWING-ACCURACY craft, DfE KS3 Working Scientifically also applies — 'make and record observations and measurements using a range of methods…; use appropriate techniques, apparatus and materials'. Its maths prerequisite is measuring/drawing angles with a protractor (KS2–KS3 maths). This is the constructional foundation that FEEDS Reflection & Refraction (the law of reflection is verified by drawing i=r).

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no content PE; SEP-anchored):** NGSS has NO national performance expectation for ray-diagram construction (it omits geometric-optics ray diagrams; nearest content framing is MS-PS4-2, reflect/absorb/transmit — not diagrams). The honest US anchor is the Science & Engineering Practice 'Developing and Using Models' — a ray diagram IS a model used to predict and explain — rather than a content standard. Ray-diagram content appears only in some US STATE standards (California, Rhode Island). So the drawing skill is UK/international-curriculum-led.

- **Operational details:** This is the accurate CONSTRUCTION of ray diagrams as a drawing craft — distinct from its sibling 'Ray Diagrams & Images' (which is the classify-real/virtual-and-apply-to-devices skill). Three canonical single-scenario constructions, each drawn with ruler + protractor: (1) PLANE-MIRROR REFLECTION — draw the incident ray to the mirror, the DASHED normal perpendicular at the point of incidence, then the reflected ray with angle of reflection MEASURED equal to the angle of incidence (both from the normal), and locate the virtual image where the reflected rays' dashed back-extensions meet. (2) REFRACTION AT A BOUNDARY — draw the normal at the boundary and show the ray bending TOWARD the normal as it passes from air into glass (and away on exit). (3) CONVEX LENS — use the principal rays to locate the image and state whether it is real or virtual. Conventions carry meaning: straight ruled rays with ARROWHEADS for direction; SOLID = real light path, DASHED = normal / construction / virtual extension.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal), reaching toward C on the convex-lens-locate step. The core is a procedural drawing-and-measurement craft — more accessible than abstract image analysis — but it demands protractor discipline and correct conventions. Success = independently drawing an accurate, correctly-labelled plane-mirror diagram (incident ray, normal, reflected ray with measured i=r, dashed virtual image) and an air→glass refraction diagram bending the right way, and using a convex-lens construction to locate an image and name it real or virtual. Watch for the signature drawing error: measuring angles from the mirror surface instead of from the normal.
bestPractices: NORMAL FIRST, ALWAYS: draw the dashed normal perpendicular AT the point of incidence before any reflected/refracted ray, and measure BOTH angles from the normal — never from the surface. This single habit prevents the commonest construction error.

Protractor discipline: place the protractor centre exactly at the point of incidence, read to whole degrees, and CHECK angle of reflection = angle of incidence by measuring, not eyeballing 'looks about equal'.

Teach the conventions as non-negotiable notation: ruled straight lines (never freehand curves), ARROWHEADS showing the direction light travels, SOLID lines for real light paths and DASHED lines for the normal and for virtual/construction extensions.

Use the two-ray principle explicitly: only two rays are needed to locate an image point — teach WHICH two (any two incident rays for a mirror; the principal rays for a lens) so pupils aren't guessing.

Predict–observe–reconcile against a real ray box: have pupils DRAW the predicted diagram first, then shine a ray box + place a mirror/glass block and overlay the real rays, reconciling any discrepancy — grounding the drawing in the phenomenon.

One scenario at a time as a repeatable template: master mirror-reflection, then single air→glass refraction (bend toward the normal), then the convex-lens principal rays — each as its own drilled routine before combining.
Insist on full labelling as part of the construction: incident ray, normal, angle i, angle r, reflected/refracted ray, and image — an unlabelled diagram is an incomplete answer.
Show a correct worked exemplar beside the pupil's attempt so they can self-check against the conventions (normal drawn? measured from normal? dashed for virtual? arrowheads?).
keyRepresentations: The dashed NORMAL with a protractor centred at the point of incidence — the reference from which i and r are measured.
Plane-mirror construction: incident ray, normal, reflected ray (measured i = r), and dashed back-extensions meeting at the virtual image behind the mirror.
Single-boundary refraction diagram: the normal at the boundary and the ray bending TOWARD the normal on entering glass (a sharp change of direction, not a curve).
Convex-lens principal-ray construction locating the image and labelling it real or virtual.
The solid / dashed / arrowhead convention itself — the notation that distinguishes real light path from construction/virtual line and shows direction of travel.
The physical toolkit: ray box + plane mirror / glass block + protractor + ruler — what the accurate diagram is drawn to match.
commonMisconceptions: Measuring angles from the mirror/surface instead of from the NORMAL — the signature drawing error; produces a reflected ray at the wrong angle.
Omitting the normal altogether, or drawing it not perpendicular / not at the point of incidence.
Drawing rays freehand or curved instead of ruled straight lines, and leaving off arrowheads so direction of travel is lost.
Using a SOLID line for the virtual image's back-extension (it should be DASHED) — conflating a real light path with a construction line.
Refraction drawn the wrong way — bending away from the normal when entering glass, or drawing a curved path rather than a sharp change of direction exactly at the boundary.
Eyeballing 'equal angles' instead of measuring, so the reflected ray is visibly unequal; sloppy scale/ruler work.
Not knowing which or how many rays to draw — thinking one ray suffices, or picking rays that don't locate the image.
Carrying over the real/virtual confusion — drawing the plane-mirror image as if real, or expecting a virtual image to sit on a screen.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13, this topic is the drawing-accuracy craft of constructing optical ray diagrams: plane-mirror reflection (incident ray, normal, reflected ray with measured angle of reflection equal to angle of incidence, and a dashed virtual image behind the mirror located where two reflected rays' back-extensions meet), refraction through a rectangular glass block (an oblique ray bends toward the normal on entering the glass and away from it on leaving; a ray along the normal does not bend), and a convex-lens principal-ray construction that locates an image and names it real or virtual. The central disciplines are: draw the dashed normal first (perpendicular at the point of incidence) and measure every angle from the normal, never from the surface; use conventions deliberately (ruled straight rays with arrowheads, solid for real light paths, dashed for the normal and virtual/construction extensions); and use two rays to locate an image point. The authentic task is hand-drawing with a physical protractor and ruler on paper with teacher feedback; a guided on-screen construction editor is a strong stand-in for the concepts but does not fully replicate the paper-and-protractor motor skill.

activities.title: Construct a plane-mirror diagram, normal first
feedback: If you measured against the mirror surface, re-place the protractor on the NORMAL: the angle you want is between the ray and the normal, not the ray and the mirror.

Check your angles by measurement — if angle r only 'looks about equal', measure both again from the normal. An angle measured from the surface is the complement (90° minus the angle from the normal), so recording a surface angle as i, or using it to draw r from the normal, gives the wrong value and the wrong reflected ray.
You need two reflected rays to locate the image point: one ray alone cannot fix where the image sits.
The back-extensions that meet to form the image must be DASHED: no real light travels behind the mirror, so a solid line there would wrongly claim a real path.

Fold the paper along the normal: an incident ray and its reflected ray should land on each other — if they bunch on one side or retrace the incident ray, the reflection is not mirrored across the normal.
activities.rationale: Drawing the normal first and measuring from it directly targets the signature construction error (measuring from the surface) and the symmetry error (reflected ray on the wrong side), while drawing two rays makes the virtual-image location a genuine intersection rather than a remembered shape.
sourceClaims: Teaching reflection/refraction ray diagrams: measure all angles from the normal (not the surface); specular reflection and the speed-change basis of refraction; the ray diagram is both cause and cure of misconceptions.

KS3 anchors the ray model for imaging in mirrors, refraction, and qualitative convex-lens focusing; Working Scientifically requires accurate measurement with appropriate apparatus (relevant to protractor drawing accuracy).
learnerActions: On paper (or a guided drawing tool), draw a mirror line and an incident ray arriving at it from an object point.
Before drawing any reflected ray, draw the dashed normal perpendicular to the mirror AT the exact point where the ray strikes.
Place the protractor centre on the point of incidence and measure the angle of incidence from the normal; record it to whole degrees.
Draw the reflected ray on the opposite side of the normal, measuring (not eyeballing) the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence.

Draw a SECOND incident ray from the same object point striking a different part of the mirror, draw its reflected ray the same way, then extend BOTH reflected rays' dashed back-extensions behind the mirror until they meet to locate the virtual image; label incident rays, normal, angle i, angle r, reflected rays, and image.
activities.intendedInsight: Both angles are measured from the normal, each reflection is symmetric about the normal, and the image behind a plane mirror is virtual — found where two reflected rays' dashed back-extensions meet, not where any real light travels.

activities.title: Refraction at an air→glass boundary and its exit
feedback: If your ray bends away from the normal on entry, you have reversed the rule — into denser glass the ray slows and bends toward the normal.

For a ray striking the boundary at an angle, passing straight through undeviated ignores refraction; show a definite bend at the boundary (only a ray along the normal, at 0° incidence, goes straight through).
Draw the change of direction as a sharp kink at the boundary line, not a smooth curve through the glass.
Rehearse the exit in the same breath as the entry: on leaving the glass back into air the ray bends away from the normal.
activities.rationale: Explicitly rehearsing both entry and exit addresses the common errors of bending the wrong way, drawing a curve, or treating the block as a window, and grounds the direction of bending in the speed-change idea.
sourceClaims: Teaching reflection/refraction ray diagrams: measure all angles from the normal (not the surface); specular reflection and the speed-change basis of refraction; the ray diagram is both cause and cure of misconceptions.
learnerActions: Draw a rectangular glass block surrounded by air and an incident ray arriving at one face at an angle (not along the normal).
Draw the normal at the boundary and measure the angle of incidence from it.
Draw the ray inside the glass bending TOWARD the normal as a sharp change of direction at the boundary (not a curve).
Continue the ray to where it LEAVES the far side of the block and draw how it bends there, stating which way and why.
Label the normal (dashed), the incident, refracted and emergent rays (solid, with arrowheads).
activities.intendedInsight: Entering an optically denser medium at an angle, light slows and bends toward the normal; on leaving into air it bends away (for a parallel-sided block the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways). Refraction is a sharp change of direction exactly at the boundary, not a gradual curve; only a ray travelling along the normal passes through without bending.

activities.title: Locate a convex-lens image with principal rays
feedback: If you drew only one ray, add a second: a single ray cannot locate an image point.
If your rays were chosen at random and don't give a clean crossing, switch to the principal rays whose behaviour you can predict.
Decide real vs virtual by whether actual light rays cross (real) or only dashed back-extensions cross (virtual) — and draw those extensions dashed.
Do not expect a virtual image to sit on a screen; only real images can be caught on a screen.
activities.rationale: Teaching which two rays to use and the real/virtual distinction prevents the 'which/how many rays' confusion and the carry-over real/virtual confusion; this step reaches toward the more demanding end of the topic.
sourceClaims: KS3 anchors the ray model for imaging in mirrors, refraction, and qualitative convex-lens focusing; Working Scientifically requires accurate measurement with appropriate apparatus (relevant to protractor drawing accuracy).
learnerActions: Draw a convex lens with its principal axis and mark the focal points on each side.

Decide and mark where the object sits relative to the focal point, since this determines whether the image is real (object beyond F) or virtual (object between F and the lens); avoid placing it exactly at F, where the rays emerge parallel and no image forms.

Draw the known principal rays from the top of an object (e.g. the ray parallel to the axis that passes through the focal point beyond the lens, and the ray through the lens centre that continues undeviated).
Find where the rays (or their extensions) cross to locate the image point.
State whether the image is real (rays actually cross) or virtual (back-extensions cross), and label the diagram.
Note that only two rays are needed to locate an image point — choose the principal rays rather than guessing arbitrary rays.
activities.intendedInsight: An image is located where two chosen rays (or their extensions) intersect; a real image forms where light actually converges, and a virtual image where only the back-extensions appear to meet — for a convex lens, an object beyond F gives a real image, an object between F and the lens gives a virtual image, and an object exactly at F gives no image.

activities.title: Predict, then check against a real ray box
feedback: If the real reflected ray and your drawn one disagree, re-check whether you measured from the normal and whether angle r truly equals angle i; also check the setup (mirror lined up with the drawn mirror line, a narrow ray, angles read at the point of incidence), since small differences can come from the apparatus rather than your drawing.
If the real refracted ray bends the opposite way to your drawing, revisit the 'into denser → bends toward normal' rule.
Treat a mismatch as information, not failure — state the specific convention or measurement that needs fixing.
activities.rationale: Predict–observe–reconcile grounds the drawing craft in the phenomenon; the source cites it as an effective remedy for drawing/optics misconceptions, including reasoning that violates the law of reflection.
sourceClaims: Documented drawing/optics misconceptions including students producing reasoning that violates the law of reflection while drawing, and inability to draw a usable ray diagram; predict-observe-reconcile / guided inquiry is the effective remedy. No NGSS national PE covers ray-diagram construction; optics appears only in some US state standards.
learnerActions: Before using any apparatus, DRAW your predicted diagram for the chosen scenario (mirror, air→glass block, or lens).
Set up a ray box with a plane mirror, glass block or convex lens (whichever matches your predicted scenario) and shine a ray, or rays, to match your scenario.
Overlay or compare the real ray path with your prediction, marking where they agree and where they differ.
Reconcile any discrepancy: adjust your understanding or re-measure, and write down what caused the difference.
activities.intendedInsight: A ray diagram is a model that should predict the real phenomenon; comparing a prediction to observed rays exposes and corrects construction errors.

activities.title: Read and apply the drawing conventions
feedback: If your diagram has no visual difference between real light and construction lines, ask 'which of these is actual light?' — if you can't tell, re-ink to the convention.
The angle of reflection is measured from the normal; the surface is a distractor baseline.
Every real ray needs an arrowhead so the direction of travel is not lost.
activities.rationale: A worked exemplar and convention-matching consolidate the notation and can catch the surface-vs-normal and single-line-style errors; this recognition/consolidation work supports but does not itself elicit independent construction.
sourceClaims: Teaching reflection/refraction ray diagrams: measure all angles from the normal (not the surface); specular reflection and the speed-change basis of refraction; the ray diagram is both cause and cure of misconceptions.
learnerActions: Match each convention to its meaning: solid line = real light path; dashed line = normal or virtual/construction extension; arrowhead = direction light travels.
Given a diagram, identify which line should be dashed and from where the angle of reflection is measured (normal vs surface).
Re-ink or correct a diagram that uses one line style for everything so that real light paths and construction lines are visually distinct.
On a correct annotated exemplar, locate and explain each element (normal, angle i, angle r, incident/reflected/refracted ray, virtual image, arrowheads).
activities.intendedInsight: The conventions carry meaning: they distinguish real light from construction lines and show direction, so a diagram without them is an incomplete answer.

constraints: The authentic objective is accurate hand-drawing with a physical protractor and ruler on paper, with teacher-checked feedback (a supervised workbook/hand-drawing task). Keep this as the classroom task.

A guided on-screen construction editor is a strong stand-in for the concepts (measure from the normal, i=r, dashed virtual, bend toward the normal) and can give immediate feedback on the child's own drawing, but it does not fully replicate the protractor-on-paper fine-motor skill or over-the-shoulder correction.
If a drawing tool offers a protractor, the child should position and read it themselves; auto-measuring would do the very skill being taught for them.
Recognition tasks (matching conventions, choosing which line is dashed) consolidate the rules and can catch errors, but they do not elicit independent construction; pair them with actual drawing.
A pre-authored annotated exemplar is a worked example and reference; because it is fixed it cannot be altered or corrected by the learner, so it supports rather than replaces a construction task.
Keep every drawn construction fully labelled (incident ray, normal, angle i, angle r, reflected/refracted ray, image); an unlabelled diagram is an incomplete answer.
Locate an image point from two rays (two reflected rays for a mirror, two principal rays for a lens); one ray cannot fix an image point.
Allow a tolerance on exact drawn angles rather than demanding pixel-perfect measurement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the PhET 'Bending Light' claim as verified:false; the interactive-tool claim is treated as unverified and is not cited as support for any activity. The other three cited claims are labelled verified:true in the source but have not been re-checked here.

The source states there is no NGSS national performance expectation for ray-diagram construction and that ray-diagram content appears only in some US state standards (e.g. California, Rhode Island); this is a curriculum-scope note, not a claim about teaching efficacy.

Original source framing described the ray diagram as 'both cause and cure of misconceptions' and the editor as able to fix 'the single commonest error fixed in the act of drawing'; claims of a single artefact being necessary or uniquely corrective have been softened to narrowly scoped proposals, since catalog fit ratings do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.
The source asserted that a static image/3D/dialogue 'cannot teach' aspects of this skill; these have been reframed as scope/affordance notes rather than universal pedagogical laws.

The source's evidence item and assess diagnostic present a single-ray plane-mirror task; locating a virtual image by intersection actually requires two reflected rays, so activity 1 has been made explicit about drawing a second ray, consistent with the stated two-ray principle.

Activity 3's convex-lens sourceClaim (source 1, measure-from-normal/refraction) supports the protractor/measurement and surface-vs-normal elements of the conventions activity but does not itself establish the solid/dashed/arrowhead notation; the notation conventions are drawing-craft practice reflected in the pedagogy rather than directly asserted by a single source claim.

probeDeeper: Show me exactly where you'd rest the protractor's centre and its zero line to measure the angle of incidence.
You've drawn the ray entering the glass. Now carry it on until it LEAVES the block on the far side — which way does it bend there, and why?
Why did you draw the normal dashed but the ray solid — what's the difference in what they represent?
If the mirror were tilted 10° steeper but the incoming ray stayed the same, would your reflected ray still land in the same place? Redraw to show it.
assess.correctAnswer: The dotted line is the NORMAL — the line perpendicular to the surface at the point the ray strikes — and angles of incidence and reflection are both measured FROM it, not from the mirror. The reflected ray leaves on the other side of the normal with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence (measured normal-to-ray on each side). Going into glass, the ray bends TOWARD the normal (it slows in the denser medium). Incident/reflected/refracted rays are drawn as solid lines with arrows; the normal and any 'image behind the mirror' construction lines are dashed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures the angle of incidence from the MIRROR SURFACE instead of the normal ('the ray is 30° from the mirror, so incidence is 30°').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist the normal is always drawn FIRST and every angle is read from it. Have them label both angles from the normal on three diagrams before drawing any reflected ray.
errorPatterns.distractor: Measure the angle between the incoming ray and the mirror surface.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked which angles to protractor, the child places it against the mirror line, giving angles that sum wrongly; equal-from-surface only coincidentally matches equal-from-normal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws the reflected ray on the SAME side of the normal as the incident ray, or straight back along it, rather than mirrored across the normal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the symmetry with a folded-paper demo (fold along the normal, incident and reflected rays land on each other) and a real mirror + ray box.
errorPatterns.distractor: The reflected ray goes back on the same side of the normal as the incoming ray.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finished diagram has both rays bunched on one side, or the ray retraces itself; the reflection doesn't 'open out' symmetrically about the normal.

errorPatterns.pattern: In the refraction half, bends the ray AWAY from the normal on entering glass, or keeps it straight — reverses or ignores the speed-change rule for entering a denser medium.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach 'into denser → slows → bends toward normal' with the ray-box-into-glass-block demo, and always rehearse the EXIT case in the same breath.
errorPatterns.distractor: Entering the glass, the ray bends away from the normal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The refracted ray inside the glass opens away from the normal (as if speeding up), or continues undeviated as through a window.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses one line style for everything — draws the normal, image and rays all solid (or all dashed) — treating the conventions as decoration rather than meaning.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the code explicitly: solid+arrow = real light; dashed = normal or apparent/behind-mirror construction. Have them re-ink one diagram to the convention.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No visual distinction between real light paths and construction lines; asked 'which of these is actual light?', the child can't tell from their own diagram.

responseLevels.gap: Ignores the normal (measures from the surface or by eye), draws a reflected/refracted ray that breaks the symmetry or bends the wrong way, and uses line styles inconsistently.
responseLevels.full: Draws the normal first, measures both angles from it, produces a symmetric reflected ray and a correctly-bent refracted ray (toward the normal on entry, and can carry it through the exit), and uses solid/dashed conventions deliberately — transferring correctly when the mirror is re-tilted or the ray must exit the block.
responseLevels.partial: Draws a plausible reflected ray with equal angles and bends refraction the right way, but measures or reasons from the surface rather than the normal in at least one step, or applies conventions without being able to justify them — struggles to extend to the exit ray or a re-tilted mirror.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a half-finished ray diagram: a mirror line, a ray arriving at it, and a dotted line drawn at 90° to the mirror where the ray hits. First tell me what that dotted line is and what it's for. Then finish the diagram — draw the reflected ray correctly, and tell me which angles you'd put your protractor on to check it's right. Then, on this second diagram of a ray going from air into a glass block, draw how the ray continues inside the glass.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The task forces the child to USE the normal as the reference (not the surface) and to deploy the solid-vs-dashed convention meaningfully — the two errors that most distinguish a child who understands the diagram from one copying a remembered shape. Because they must both interpret the given normal AND produce a measured reflected ray plus a refracted ray, guessing a 'mirror-image V' cannot pass: the protractor question checks whether they measure from the right baseline.
